title: Al-'Afuww, the Pardoner
hookLine: the Pardoner, who erases sins entirely
tomorrow: tender toward someone who wronged you: strength, or weakness?

cards: Delete a photo and, on some phones, it isn't gone. It sits in a recently deleted folder, waiting to be dragged back out. Erasing it for real takes a second step.
Yesterday's question was about a prayer that asks for that second step. Aisha asked the Prophet, peace be upon him: if I knew which night was Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, what should I say?
He handed her one short line. And the odd thing is the word in the middle of it. It isn't the usual word for forgiveness.

teach.h: YOU LOVE TO PARDON, SO PARDON ME.
teach.b: Here's the line, in Arabic: Allahumma innaka 'afuwwun tuhibbul 'afwa fa'fu 'anni. O Allah, You are the Pardoner, You love to pardon, so pardon me.
The more familiar word for forgiveness is maghfira, and the Qur'an uses it too. So why this one?

Some scholars explain the difference this way: maghfira covers a sin, like a veil drawn over it, while 'afw wipes it out, the way wind smooths away footprints in sand. Covered is still there, underneath. Wiped is gone.
That's today's Name, Al-'Afuww, the Pardoner.
The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's words: "And He it is Who accepteth repentance from His bondmen, and pardoneth the evil deeds." Now look at the middle of the prayer again: You love to pardon.
Not a God who pardons reluctantly, once you've begged enough, but one who loves doing it. And here's something to tell a friend tonight.
The Qur'an says of that night, "The Night of Power is better than a thousand months."
Asked what to say on it, the Prophet didn't give Aisha a long list. He gave her the delete key.

how: Muslims seeking Laylat al-Qadr in the last nights of Ramadan repeat the line taught to Aisha: Allahumma innaka 'afuwwun tuhibbul 'afwa fa'fu 'anni.

o: the Pardoner, who wipes a wrong away
the Witness, who records every deed
the Patient One, who waits for apologies

games.q: the line for the night — tap the pairs.
p: a sin covered, like a veil
a sin wiped away, like tracks in sand

s: 'afw and maghfira are just two ways of saying the same thing
some scholars draw a line: maghfira covers a sin, 'afw wipes it out.
the prayer for Laylat al-Qadr that the Prophet taught Aisha is one short line
You are the Pardoner, You love to pardon, so pardon me.
the Qur'an calls the Night of Power better than a thousand months
"The Night of Power is better than a thousand months."

games.q: your little brother broke your headphones last month. he apologized and you said 'it's fine.' now, mid-argument, it's right on your tongue again. what does 'afw ask of you?
o: bring it up; pardon covered it, but it's still on file.
leave it erased; pardoned means it doesn't come back as ammo.
make him apologize again first, then pardon him properly.
games.why: covered is still underneath; wiped is gone. the Pardoner loves to pardon, and the prayer asks for the trace to go, not to be saved for later.

practice: Close your eyes and let one thing you keep replaying come to mind, something you did, not something done to you. If you pray, say the line slowly inside: You love to pardon, so pardon me.
Or simply let the memory sit without pressing play on it again, and feel what it's like to leave it unreplayed.

wordCard.voice: Al-'Afuww. The Pardoner, who doesn't just cover a wrong but wipes the trace away, and loves to.

orig.note: Arabic: the Pardoner, a Name of Allah; the same root gives 'afw, pardon, in the prayer for Laylat al-Qadr.

carryVoice: Keep it near: erased, not filed in a folder somewhere to be dragged back out later. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3513; Sunan Ibn Majah 3850 (Aisha asks what to say on Laylat al-Qadr)

sources.q: And He it is Who accepteth repentance from His bondmen, and pardoneth the evil deeds
